title: UI/UX Design Basics for Marketers
subtitle: Design landing pages, flows and forms people can actually use — mobile-first, accessible and tested with real users
description:
Marketers shape user experience every day: landing pages, sign-up forms, checkout flows, emails and the pages behind every ad. Small UX problems quietly waste budget — confusing navigation, slow mobile pages, forms that ask too much, buttons people cannot find. This course gives marketers, creators and small-agency teams a practical foundation in UI and UX design without needing to become full-time product designers.

You will learn usability heuristics, user flows and information architecture, UX writing, wireframing and prototyping, landing-page UX, mobile-first design, ethical persuasion, and the essentials of accessibility under WCAG 2.2. Finally, you will learn to test with real users, read analytics and run sensible A/B tests, and turn findings into improvements. Every lesson includes templates and a hands-on activity you can apply to your own pages.
outcomes: Evaluate pages and flows using established usability heuristics
Map user flows and structure navigation so people find what they need
Write clear interface copy for buttons, forms, errors and empty states
Create wireframes and simple prototypes to test ideas before building
Design mobile-first landing pages with strong message match and ethical persuasion
Apply WCAG 2.2 accessibility basics to pages, forms and content
Run lightweight usability tests and interpret analytics and A/B tests responsibly

lessons.title: UI, UX and why marketers should care
lessons.body:
### Two terms, one experience

- **User experience (UX)** is the whole experience a person has when trying to achieve something with your product, site or service: whether they can find what they need, understand it, trust it and complete their task without frustration.
- **User interface (UI)** is the part they see and interact with: layouts, buttons, forms, typography, colours, icons, states and feedback.

UI is a big part of UX, but UX also includes content, speed, reliability, customer service, pricing clarity and even what happens after a purchase.

### Why this is a marketing problem

Marketing spends money to bring people to a page. UX determines what happens next.

- An ad can be brilliant, but if the landing page is slow, confusing or broken on mobile, the budget is wasted.
- A sign-up form that asks for too much information loses people who were ready to convert.
- Confusing pricing pages create support tickets and abandoned carts.
- Poor accessibility excludes customers and can create legal exposure.

Improving UX is often one of the most cost-effective ways to improve marketing results, because it increases the value of traffic you already pay for.

### The UX mindset: you are not the user

The most important principle in UX is simple: **you are not your user**. You know your product, your jargon and where everything is. Visitors do not. They arrive distracted, on a small screen, often from an ad or a social post, with a specific question in mind.

Three habits of the UX mindset:

1. **Start from the user's goal**, not the company's message. "What is this person trying to do right now?"
2. **Observe behaviour, not opinions.** What people do on a page is more reliable than what they say they like.
3. **Iterate.** Treat pages as hypotheses; test, learn and improve.

### Where marketers touch UX

| Marketing asset | UX questions |
|---|---|
| Landing pages | Does the page match the ad's promise? Is the next step obvious? |
| Forms and sign-ups | Are we asking only what we need? Are errors clear? |
| Email and SMS | Is the call to action clear on mobile? Are links easy to tap? |
| Website navigation | Can people find pricing, contact and key information fast? |
| Checkout and booking | Are costs clear up front? Are there unnecessary steps? |
| Social profiles and link-in-bio pages | Is the path from post to action short and clear? |
| Chat and customer support | Can people get help when stuck? |

### A simple UX quality model

Many teams use a set of qualities to judge an experience. A practical version:

```
Useful      — Does it meet a real need?
Usable      — Can people complete tasks easily?
Findable    — Can people locate what they need?
Credible    — Do people trust it?
Accessible  — Can people with disabilities use it?
Desirable   — Does it look and feel appealing and on-brand?
Fast        — Does it load and respond quickly, especially on mobile?
```

If any one fails, the experience fails for someone.

### Worked example: a webinar sign-up

A creator runs ads for a free webinar. Clicks are healthy, but few people register.

UX review findings:

- The ad promises "Grow on LinkedIn in 30 days" but the landing page headline says "Welcome to my community" — weak message match.
- The registration form asks for name, email, phone, company, job title, country, and "How did you hear about us?".
- On mobile, the register button is below a long biography.
- The page loads slowly because of a large background video.

Fixes: headline repeats the ad promise; form reduced to name and email (optional phone for reminders with clear consent); register button repeated near the top on mobile; video replaced with a compressed image. The creator then measures registrations per visitor over the next campaign rather than assuming the fixes worked.

### Common mistakes

- Treating UX as "making it pretty".
- Designing from the company's perspective ("what we want to say") instead of the user's goal.
- Judging pages on desktop only, when most social traffic is mobile.
- Changing many things based on opinions without measuring.

### Summary

UX is the whole experience of achieving a goal; UI is the visible, interactive layer. Marketers influence UX constantly, and improving it multiplies the value of traffic. Adopt the UX mindset — you are not the user — and judge experiences on usefulness, usability, findability, credibility, accessibility, desirability and speed.

video.script: Every time you run an ad, send an email or post a link, you're sending people into an experience. What happens next is user experience, or UX. UX is the whole experience someone has when they try to get something done: finding information, understanding it, trusting it and completing a task without frustration. The user interface, or UI, is the part they see and touch — the layout, the buttons, the forms, the colours and the feedback when they tap something. UI is a big part of UX, but UX also includes speed, content, pricing clarity and what happens after someone converts. Why should marketers care? Because marketing buys attention, and UX decides whether that attention turns into results. A great ad pointing to a slow, confusing mobile page wastes money. A form that asks for ten fields loses people who were ready to sign up. The most important idea in UX is simple: you are not your user. You know your product and your jargon. Your visitors arrive distracted, on a phone, with one question in mind. So start from their goal, watch what people actually do rather than what they say, and treat every page as a hypothesis you can improve. Here's a quick check you can run on any page. Is it useful? Is it easy to use? Can people find what they need? Do they trust it? Can people with disabilities use it? Does it feel appealing and on-brand? And is it fast, especially on mobile? If any one of those fails, the experience fails for someone. In this course, you'll learn to spot these problems and fix them.

keyTakeaways: UX is the whole experience of achieving a goal; UI is the visible, interactive layer.
Improving UX increases the value of traffic you already pay for.
You are not your user — start from their goal and observe behaviour.
Judge experiences on usefulness, usability, findability, credibility, accessibility, desirability and speed.

lessons.title: The 10 usability heuristics in practice
lessons.body:
### A shared checklist for good interfaces

In the 1990s, usability expert Jakob Nielsen published ten general principles for interaction design, known as **usability heuristics**. They remain one of the most widely used tools for evaluating interfaces quickly. A heuristic evaluation — reviewing a page against these principles — takes little time and reliably uncovers common problems.

### The ten heuristics with marketing examples

| # | Heuristic | What it means | Marketing example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Visibility of system status | Keep users informed about what's happening | "Sending…" then "Thanks! Check your inbox" after a form submit; progress steps in checkout |
| 2 | Match between system and the real world | Use users' language and familiar concepts | "Book a call" instead of "Initiate consultation workflow" |
| 3 | User control and freedom | Provide clear ways to undo, go back or exit | Easy-to-find close button on pop-ups; editable cart |
| 4 | Consistency and standards | Follow platform and internal conventions | Links look like links; the logo returns home; buttons look the same site-wide |
| 5 | Error prevention | Prevent problems before they occur | Date pickers instead of free text; confirming before deleting |
| 6 | Recognition rather than recall | Make options visible instead of relying on memory | Showing selected plan details at checkout; recently viewed items |
| 7 | Flexibility and efficiency of use | Support both novices and experts | Autofill, saved details, shortcuts for returning customers |
| 8 | Aesthetic and minimalist design | Remove information that competes with what matters | One primary call to action per section |
| 9 | Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors | Plain-language error messages with solutions | "That email looks incomplete — did you mean name@gmail.com?" |
| 10 | Help and documentation | Provide easy-to-find help when needed | FAQs near pricing; chat link during checkout |

### Running a quick heuristic evaluation

1. **Define the task** you're evaluating ("Register for the webinar on mobile").
2. **Walk through the task** as a new user would, ideally on the device your audience uses.
3. **Note each problem**, the heuristic it breaks, and where it happens.
4. **Rate severity** — for example 0 (not a problem) to 4 (blocks the task).
5. **Recommend a fix** for each.
6. **Ideally, have two or three people evaluate independently**, then combine findings; different people spot different problems.

```
Heuristic evaluation log
Task: ________________________   Device: ________
No Location        Problem                       Heuristic  Severity  Fix
1  Form            No confirmation after submit   H1         3        Add success message + email
2  Pricing         "SKU tiers" jargon             H2         2        Rename to "Plans"
3  Pop-up          Close button tiny, low contrast H3        3        Larger, clear close button
```

### Severity helps prioritise

Not every issue matters equally. Prioritise:

- **Frequency:** how many users hit it?
- **Impact:** how badly does it block them?
- **Persistence:** is it a one-time annoyance or a repeated one?

Fix high-severity, high-frequency issues first. A missing confirmation message on a paid-traffic form may matter more than a slightly inconsistent icon.

### Limitations

Heuristic evaluation is fast and cheap but it is expert judgement, not user evidence. It misses problems specific to your audience's knowledge, context or language, and it can produce false alarms. Combine it with usability testing and analytics (covered later in the course).

### Worked example: a small e-commerce store

Task: "Buy a phone case on mobile."

Findings:

- H1: After tapping "Add to cart", nothing visible changes — users tap again and add two cases.
- H2: Shipping is called "fulfilment fee".
- H4: Some buttons are rounded and green, others square and grey.
- H5: The phone model is typed as free text, leading to mistakes.
- H9: Card errors say "Transaction failed (code 51)".
- H10: No delivery information until the last step.

Fixes: a toast message and cart badge update; "Shipping" wording; one button style; a model dropdown; human-readable payment errors with next steps; delivery times shown on product pages.

### Common mistakes

- Evaluating on desktop when most customers use mobile.
- Listing problems without severity, so teams fix trivial issues first.
- Treating heuristics as rigid rules rather than guides.
- Skipping real user testing because "we already did a heuristic review".

### Summary

Nielsen's ten heuristics give you a fast, structured way to review any page or flow. Define a task, walk through it on the right device, log problems with the heuristic, severity and fix, and prioritise by frequency and impact — then validate with real users.
keyTakeaways: Nielsen's ten heuristics are a fast, widely used checklist for evaluating interfaces.
Evaluate specific tasks on the device your audience actually uses.
Log each problem with the heuristic, severity and a recommended fix.
Heuristic reviews complement — but don't replace — testing with real users.

knowledgeCheck.question: After submitting a form, nothing on the page changes. Which heuristic is violated?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Users need feedback about what happened; without it they may resubmit or leave.

knowledgeCheck.question: A checkout error reads 'Error 0x80045'. Which heuristic does a better message address?
options: Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Error messages should explain the problem in plain language and suggest a solution.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a key limitation of heuristic evaluation?
options: It relies on expert judgement and can miss audience-specific problems, so it should be combined with user testing
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It's fast and cheap but not a substitute for evidence from real users.

lessons.activity: Run a heuristic evaluation of one key task on your website or a client's, on a mobile phone. Log at least six problems with heuristic, severity and fix, and pick the top three to address.

lessons.title: Understanding users: goals, jobs and lightweight research
lessons.body:
### Design starts with people

Every UX decision rests on assumptions about users: who they are, what they want, what they already know, and what worries them. Better assumptions — grounded in evidence — lead to better pages. You don't need a research department; lightweight methods get you most of the way.

### Goals, tasks and context

For each key audience, capture:

- **Goal:** what they ultimately want ("Get more clients for my salon").
- **Task:** what they are trying to do on this page right now ("Compare booking software prices").
- **Context:** device, place, time pressure, language, connection quality.
- **Anxieties:** what might stop them ("Hidden fees?", "Is my data safe?", "Will this work in my country?").
- **Knowledge:** familiarity with the category and jargon.

### Jobs to be done

The **jobs-to-be-done** idea frames users' needs as progress they're trying to make: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]."

Example: "When I'm launching a new product, I want to get a professional landing page live in a day, so I can start taking pre-orders before my competitors."

Job statements help you prioritise content: this user needs speed, templates and payment setup, not a long history of the company.

### Proto-personas

Full research-based personas take time. **Proto-personas** are quick, assumption-based profiles created from what the team knows, then validated over time.

```
Proto-persona
Name/label:     "Busy salon owner" (avoid stereotypes; focus on behaviour)
Context:        Runs a 3-chair salon in Lahore; manages bookings on WhatsApp
Goal:           Reduce no-shows and admin time
Tasks on site:  Understand features, check price in local currency, see if it works with WhatsApp
Anxieties:      Cost, learning curve, staff adoption
Channels:       Instagram, Facebook groups, word of mouth
Evidence:       3 sales calls, 20 support chats (update as research grows)
```

Mark which parts are assumptions and which are evidenced.

### Lightweight research methods

| Method | What it gives you | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| Customer interviews (5–8) | Motivations, language, anxieties | Low–medium |
| Support tickets, chats, DMs, reviews | Real problems in customers' words | Low |
| Sales call notes | Objections and decision criteria | Low |
| On-site surveys (one question) | Why people visit, what's missing | Low |
| Analytics | What people do, where they drop | Low–medium |
| Search queries (site search and search engines) | What people look for | Low |
| Usability tests | Where people struggle | Medium |

### Interview tips

- Ask about **past behaviour**, not hypothetical futures: "Tell me about the last time you booked a…" rather than "Would you use…?"
- Ask open questions and follow up with "Why?" and "Tell me more".
- Avoid leading questions ("Don't you think this is easy?").
- Record (with consent) or take detailed notes; note exact phrases people use.
- Respect privacy: collect only what you need, explain how notes are used, and follow data-protection rules in your market.

### Turning research into design decisions

Research is only useful if it changes something. After collecting insights:

1. Cluster notes into themes (affinity mapping).
2. Write insights as statements: "Salon owners worry staff won't adopt new tools."
3. Turn insights into design implications: "Show a 'staff app in 5 minutes' video and a testimonial from a salon manager."
4. Prioritise implications for the pages that matter most.

### Worked example: a coaching programme page

Research: 6 interviews and 50 DM questions. Themes: price uncertainty, time commitment, "Is this for beginners?", payment options in local currency.

Design implications: a "Who this is for / not for" section; weekly time commitment stated clearly; price shown in multiple currencies where appropriate with clear instalment terms; FAQ addressing beginner concerns in the exact language people used.

### Common mistakes

- Designing for "everyone".
- Personas based on demographics only, with no goals or anxieties.
- Asking people to predict future behaviour.
- Doing research and then ignoring it.

### Research ethics and privacy

Treat research participants with respect. Explain why you are talking to them, how long it will take and how notes or recordings will be used, and get their consent before recording. Store notes securely, remove personal details you do not need, and delete recordings when the project ends. Pay or reward participants fairly for their time, and never use research sessions as a disguised sales pitch.

### Summary

Capture users' goals, tasks, context, anxieties and knowledge; express needs as jobs to be done; start with proto-personas and validate them; use lightweight research sources; and translate insights into specific design implications.
keyTakeaways: Capture goals, tasks, context, anxieties and knowledge for each key audience.
Jobs-to-be-done statements focus design on the progress users want to make.
Proto-personas are quick starting points — mark assumptions and validate them.
Interview about past behaviour, avoid leading questions and turn insights into design implications.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which interview question is most useful?
options: 'Don't you think our design is easy?'
'Would you use an app like this?'
'Tell me about the last time you booked an appointment for your salon.'
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Questions about specific past behaviour yield reliable insight; hypothetical and leading questions do not.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes a proto-persona different from a research-based persona?
options: It's built quickly from team knowledge and assumptions, to be validated over time
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Proto-personas are quick, assumption-based profiles built from what the team already knows, then validated and updated as research accumulates; photos and completeness are not what defines them.

knowledgeCheck.question: Research shows users worry about hidden fees. What's the best design implication?
options: Show total costs clearly and early, including fees
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Addressing the anxiety directly with transparent pricing builds trust.

lessons.activity: Review 20 recent customer messages, reviews or support tickets. Cluster them into themes, write three insight statements and one design implication for each.

modules.summary: Map user flows and journeys, organise navigation and content, and write clear microcopy for buttons, forms and errors.

lessons.title: User flows and journey maps
lessons.body:
### Seeing the whole path

Marketers often design single pages, but users experience **paths**: an ad, a landing page, a form, an email confirmation, a reminder, a purchase. Problems frequently hide between pages. User flows and journey maps make those paths visible.

### User flows

A **user flow** is a diagram of the steps a user takes to complete a task, including decisions and alternative paths.

Basic notation:

```
[Entry point] → (Page/screen) → {Decision?} → (Page) → [Goal]
                                   ↓ no
                               (Alternative path)
```

Example — webinar registration from Instagram:

```
[Instagram story ad] → (Landing page) → {Registered before?}
    ↓ no                                       ↓ yes
(Form: name + email) → (Thank-you page + calendar link) → [Registered]
    ↓ error
(Inline error message) → back to form
[Registered] → (Confirmation email) → (Reminder 1 day before) → (Reminder 1 hour before) → [Attends]
```

What to look for:

- **Number of steps** — can any be removed or combined?
- **Dead ends** — pages with no clear next step.
- **Error paths** — what happens when something goes wrong?
- **Channel switches** — moving from app to browser, social to website, email to WhatsApp — each switch risks drop-off.
- **Logged-in vs new users** — different paths.

### Happy path and edge cases

The **happy path** is the ideal route with no problems. Real users take many others:

- Payment declined.
- Email typed wrongly.
- Arriving from a shared link on a different device.
- Returning later to finish.
- Using a screen reader or keyboard only.
- Slow or interrupted connections.

Design at least the most common edge cases explicitly.

### Journey maps

A **customer journey map** zooms out further, capturing stages, actions, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the whole relationship.

| Stage | Aware | Consider | Sign up | Onboard | Use/Renew |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Actions | Sees reel | Visits site, reads reviews | Starts trial | Sets up account | Uses weekly |
| Touchpoints | Instagram | Website, Google reviews | Sign-up form | Emails, app | App, support |
| Thoughts | "Could this help me?" | "Is it worth the price?" | "Is this safe?" | "How do I start?" | "Is it still worth it?" |
| Feelings | Curious | Unsure | Anxious | Overwhelmed | Satisfied / frustrated |
| Opportunities | Clear promise | Transparent pricing, proof | Minimal form, trust signals | Guided setup | Tips, renewal reminders |

Journey maps help marketing, sales, product and support teams see their part of the same experience.

### Creating a flow: step by step

1. Choose one important task and entry point.
2. List every screen, message and decision.
3. Walk the flow yourself on mobile, taking screenshots.
4. Mark friction points: extra steps, unclear copy, slow loads, errors.
5. Add analytics data where available (drop-off at each step).
6. Propose a simplified flow.

### Worked example: a consultation booking flow

Original: Facebook ad → homepage → Services page → Contact page → long contact form → "We'll get back to you" → email back-and-forth to choose a time.

Problems: too many steps, the ad lands on the homepage (weak message match), no instant booking, uncertainty after submitting.

Redesign: ad → dedicated landing page matching the ad → embedded scheduler showing available times in the visitor's time zone → short form (name, email, one qualifying question) → confirmation page and calendar invite → reminder emails/SMS with consent.

### Common mistakes

- Designing screens in isolation.
- Ignoring error and edge-case paths.
- Forgetting post-conversion steps (confirmation, onboarding).
- Mapping the journey the company wishes existed rather than the real one.

### Measuring a flow

Once a flow is mapped, attach numbers to it. Most analytics tools can show how many people reach each step and where they leave. Even rough figures change priorities: a step that loses half of mobile visitors deserves attention before a cosmetic issue elsewhere. Record the baseline before you change anything, so you can compare results fairly afterwards and explain the improvement to your team or client.

### Summary

Use user flows to map task paths, including decisions and errors, and journey maps to see stages, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the relationship. Walk flows on mobile, mark friction, and simplify.
keyTakeaways: Users experience paths, not pages — map them.
User flows show steps, decisions, errors and channel switches for one task.
Journey maps capture stages, actions, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the relationship.
Design common edge cases, not just the happy path.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the 'happy path' in a user flow?
options: The ideal route through a task with no problems
A path for returning customers only
The path with the most steps
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It's the ideal route; real users also encounter edge cases that need design.

knowledgeCheck.question: A consultation flow requires email back-and-forth to choose a time. What is the most effective improvement?
options: Ask users to call during office hours only
Embed a scheduler showing available times so users book instantly
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An embedded scheduler lets people book instantly, removing email back-and-forth and the uncertainty of waiting; more fields or phone-only booking add friction.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which element belongs in a customer journey map but usually not in a simple user flow?
options: Users' thoughts and feelings at each stage
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Journey maps capture emotional and cognitive context across stages.

lessons.activity: Map the flow from one of your ads or social posts to conversion, including at least two edge cases. Mark every friction point and draw a simplified version.

lessons.title: Information architecture and navigation
lessons.body:
### Helping people find things

**Information architecture (IA)** is the structure and labelling of content so people can find what they need and understand where they are. Poor IA shows up as "I couldn't find your prices", high bounce rates, and lots of support questions that the website already answers somewhere.

### Core IA concepts

| Concept | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Organisation | How content is grouped | By service, by audience, by task |
| Labelling | What groups and links are called | "Pricing" vs "Investment" |
| Navigation | How people move around | Header menu, footer, breadcrumbs, search |
| Search | Finding by query | Site search, filters |
| Hierarchy | Levels of content | Home → Services → Service detail |

### Labels in users' words

Labels are one of the biggest findability factors. Use words your users use (from interviews, search queries and support tickets), not internal jargon or clever branding.

| Weak label | Clearer label |
|---|---|
| Solutions | Services |
| Investment | Pricing |
| Our Journey | About us |
| Resources Hub | Guides / Blog |
| Connect | Contact |

Creative labels can be fine for brand personality in content, but navigation should be clear.

### Navigation patterns

- **Header navigation:** 4–7 top-level items is a common, manageable range for small business sites. Put the most important tasks first.
- **Primary call to action** in the header (e.g. "Book a call", "Start free trial").
- **Mobile navigation:** a menu icon with a clear label or recognisable icon; keep the key CTA visible outside the menu if possible.
- **Footer:** secondary links — policies, careers, social links, contact details.
- **Breadcrumbs:** for deeper sites (shops, knowledge bases).
- **Search:** essential for large content libraries and shops.

### Organising content: card sorting

**Card sorting** is a simple research method to understand how users group content:

- **Open card sort:** users group topics and name the groups themselves — reveals mental models and labels.
- **Closed card sort:** users place topics into predefined categories — tests your structure.

Can be done with paper cards or online tools, with even a small number of participants.

**Tree testing** checks whether people can find items in a proposed menu structure (text-only), before any visual design.

### Sitemaps

A **sitemap** (for planning, not the XML file for search engines) shows every page and its hierarchy:

```
Home
├── Services
│   ├── Brand identity
│   ├── Social media content
│   └── Websites
├── Work (case studies)
├── Pricing
├── About
├── Blog
└── Contact / Book a call
```

For marketing sites, keep hierarchy shallow — key pages should be reachable within one or two taps.

### Landing pages and navigation

Dedicated campaign landing pages often **remove or reduce main navigation** to keep focus on one conversion goal. This can improve conversion but should still allow users control: keep the logo link or a minimal footer, and provide essential information (pricing, privacy policy, contact) so trust isn't harmed.

### Multilingual and RTL considerations

For sites serving English, Arabic and Urdu audiences:

- Provide an obvious language switcher (language names in their own script: "English", "العربية", "اردو").
- Mirror navigation for right-to-left languages.
- Keep equivalent structure across languages so users can switch without getting lost.

### Worked example: an agency website restructure

Problem: prospects couldn't find pricing or examples; menu had nine items with creative labels ("The Lab", "Our DNA", "Let's Talk Magic").

Process: reviewed site search and sales call questions; ran an open card sort with eight clients; tree-tested a new structure.

New IA: Services, Work, Pricing, About, Blog, plus a "Book a call" button. Case studies filterable by industry. Result tracked: more visits to pricing and case studies, and fewer "what do you charge?" emails (measured over the following quarter).

### Common mistakes

- Clever labels that hide meaning.
- Too many top-level menu items.
- Organising by internal team structure instead of user tasks.
- Hiding essential information in footers or PDFs.

### Summary

Organise and label content in users' words, keep navigation focused and shallow, use card sorting and tree testing to validate structures, plan with a sitemap, and handle landing-page and multilingual navigation deliberately.
keyTakeaways: Information architecture is how content is organised and labelled so people can find it.
Use labels in users' words, not internal jargon or clever branding.
Card sorting reveals mental models; tree testing validates a menu structure.
Keep navigation shallow and focused; plan landing-page and multilingual navigation deliberately.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which navigation label is usually clearest for a pricing page?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Plain, familiar labels are found faster than creative alternatives.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does a tree test evaluate?
options: Whether users can find items in a proposed navigation structure
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Tree testing checks findability in a text-only menu structure before visual design.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why do many campaign landing pages reduce main navigation?
options: Because navigation is illegal on landing pages
To keep focus on one conversion goal while still providing essential trust information
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Reducing distraction can help conversion, but essential information and control should remain.

lessons.activity: Draw a sitemap for your website or a client's. Rewrite any unclear navigation labels using words from customer messages, and ask three people to find two items using only the new labels.

lessons.title: UX writing, microcopy and forms
lessons.body:
### Words are interface

Buttons, labels, error messages, hints, empty states and confirmation messages are all **microcopy**. Good microcopy is often the cheapest UX improvement: changing words can make a form clearer, reduce errors and build trust — without redesigning anything.

### Principles of UX writing

1. **Clear before clever.** Say exactly what happens.
2. **Concise.** Remove words that don't help the user act.
3. **Useful.** Answer the question users have at that moment.
4. **Consistent.** Same term for the same thing everywhere ("Sign in" everywhere, not mixed with "Log in").
5. **Human.** Match brand voice, but never at the expense of clarity.
6. **Inclusive.** Plain language, no idioms that don't translate, avoid blaming users.

### Buttons and calls to action

Buttons should describe the action or outcome:

| Weak | Better |
|---|---|
| Submit | Get my free guide |
| Click here | Download the checklist |
| Continue | Continue to payment |
| OK | Delete project |
| Learn more (everywhere) | See pricing / Read case study |

Use verbs. Where risk exists, clarify cost and commitment near the button ("Start free trial — no card needed", if true).

### Forms: ask less, explain more

Forms are where many conversions die. Principles:

- **Ask only what you need now.** Every field adds effort. Collect extra information later if genuinely needed.
- **Explain why** for sensitive fields ("We'll only use your phone number for appointment reminders").
- **Visible labels above fields** — don't rely on placeholder text alone, which disappears when typing and often has poor contrast.
- **Mark optional fields** (or required fields) consistently.
- **Use the right input types** — email keyboards for email, numeric keypad for phone numbers, date pickers where helpful.
- **Group related fields** and use a single column on mobile.
- **Support autofill** and international formats (names, addresses, phone numbers vary widely across countries).
- **Consent:** where marketing consent is needed, use clear, unticked opt-in checkboxes and link to privacy information, in line with data-protection laws such as GDPR/UK GDPR and applicable local laws in your markets.

### Error messages

Good error messages are:

- **Specific:** say what went wrong.
- **Helpful:** say how to fix it.
- **Timely:** shown inline, near the field, ideally after the user leaves the field or submits.
- **Polite:** no blame ("You entered an invalid…" → "Please enter…").
- **Accessible:** not only red colour — include text and an icon; make errors announced to screen readers.

```
Error message template
[What happened] + [How to fix it]
"Your card was declined. Please check the details or try another card."
"That email address is missing an '@'. Please check and try again."
"Passwords need at least 8 characters."
```

### Empty states, confirmations and loading

- **Empty states** ("No saved items yet") are opportunities to guide: "No saved items yet — tap the heart on any product to save it."
- **Confirmations** should confirm and set expectations: "You're booked for Thursday at 3 pm. We've sent the details to amina@example.com."
- **Loading messages** reassure: "Processing payment — please don't close this page."

### Localisation

For multilingual audiences, write microcopy for each language rather than literal translation; watch for text expansion (German, for example) or different lengths in Arabic and Urdu; and ensure buttons can accommodate longer text.

### Worked example: a newsletter sign-up

Before: headline "Subscribe"; fields for first name, last name, email, phone, city, date of birth; a pre-ticked box "Send me offers from partners"; button "Submit"; error "Invalid input".

After: headline "Get one practical marketing tip every Tuesday"; fields: first name (optional), email; unticked consent for partner offers removed entirely; button "Send me the tips"; error "Please enter an email address like name@example.com"; confirmation "Almost done! Check your inbox to confirm your subscription."

### Common mistakes

- Generic buttons ("Submit", "Click here").
- Placeholder-only labels.
- Asking for unnecessary personal data.
- Pre-ticked consent boxes and vague privacy statements.
- Error messages that blame or confuse.

### A microcopy style sheet

Consistency is easier with a short style sheet. List the terms you use ("Sign in", "Basket" or "Cart", "Plan" or "Package"), your capitalisation rule for buttons, how you write dates, times and prices for each market, and a few approved examples of error and confirmation messages. Share it with everyone who writes for your site, emails and apps, including freelancers and translators.

### Summary

Treat words as interface: write clear, concise, consistent microcopy; use action-specific buttons; minimise and explain form fields; write specific, helpful, accessible errors; and design empty states and confirmations to guide users.
keyTakeaways: Microcopy is often the cheapest, fastest UX improvement.
Buttons should describe the action or outcome using verbs.
Ask only for what you need, use visible labels and explain sensitive fields.
Error messages should say what happened and how to fix it, without relying on colour alone.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which button text is best for a form that sends a free guide?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Action-specific, outcome-focused labels tell users exactly what happens.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why shouldn't forms rely only on placeholder text as labels?
options: They disappear when typing and often have poor contrast, hurting usability and accessibility
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Visible labels remain available as users type and review entries.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which error message is most helpful?
options: 'That email address is missing an @. Please check and try again.'
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It explains what went wrong and how to fix it, politely.

lessons.activity: Audit one form you own: remove any unnecessary field, rewrite the button, labels and at least two error messages using the template, and check that consent is clear and unticked.

modules.title: Wireframes, UI patterns and prototypes
modules.summary: Sketch and wireframe layouts, apply UI fundamentals and design-system thinking, and build simple prototypes to test ideas.

lessons.title: Sketching and wireframing
lessons.body:
### Think in structure before style

A **wireframe** is a simplified layout of a page or screen that shows structure, content priority and functionality — without final colours, images or polished typography. Wireframes let you agree on *what goes where and why* before spending time on visual design or development.

### Fidelity levels

| Fidelity | What it looks like | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Sketch (paper or whiteboard) | Boxes and scribbles | Exploring many ideas in minutes |
| Low-fidelity wireframe | Grey boxes, placeholder text, basic labels | Agreeing structure and content priority |
| Mid-fidelity wireframe | Real headlines and copy, real form fields, grid | Testing flows and content |
| High-fidelity mock-up | Final visuals, brand, images | Visual approval and handoff |

Moving too quickly to high fidelity makes stakeholders comment on colours and photos instead of structure. Start low.

### Content-first wireframing

Wireframes work best when they use **real content** (or close to it). Lorem ipsum hides problems — a headline that looks fine as placeholder may be twice as long in reality.

Before wireframing, write a **content priority list**:

```
Landing page content priority (example: online course)
1. Headline — the core promise
2. Subheadline — who it's for + outcome
3. Primary CTA — "Enrol now" / "Join the waitlist"
4. Proof — testimonials, results, logos (real, with permission)
5. What you'll learn — 3–6 outcomes
6. Curriculum overview
7. Instructor credibility
8. Pricing and payment options
9. FAQ — objections
10. Final CTA
```

The order reflects what users need to decide, not what the company wants to say first.

### Mobile-first wireframing

Start with the **mobile wireframe**. A narrow screen forces prioritisation — there is only one column, so you must decide what comes first. Then expand to tablet and desktop, where content can sit side by side.

Mobile wireframe checks:

- Is the primary message and CTA visible without scrolling far?
- Are tap targets large and well spaced?
- Does every section earn its place?

### Wireframing conventions

- Boxes with an "X" = images.
- Horizontal lines = text blocks.
- Rounded rectangles = buttons (label them).
- Annotations explain behaviour ("Opens scheduler in modal", "Sticky on mobile").
- Use a grid and consistent spacing even in low fidelity.

Tools: paper, whiteboards, and digital design tools (Figma-style tools, dedicated wireframing tools, even slides). The tool matters less than the thinking.

### Annotating wireframes

Annotations turn wireframes into communication tools for developers, copywriters and stakeholders:

```
Annotation examples
[1] Headline: max 10 words; test variant B next month
[2] CTA: scrolls to pricing section on click
[3] Testimonials: carousel on mobile, 3-column on desktop; real customers only
[4] Form: name + email; inline validation; success message replaces form
[5] Sticky CTA bar appears after 50% scroll on mobile
```

### Worked example: a service business homepage

A cleaning company in Dubai wants a new homepage.

1. Research showed customers mainly want: price estimate, availability, trust (vetted staff), and easy booking (often via WhatsApp).
2. Content priority: headline + instant price estimate widget; "Book now" and "Chat on WhatsApp" CTAs; trust signals (vetting, insurance, reviews); services; how it works (3 steps); areas covered; FAQ.
3. Mobile sketch: 10 minutes, three variations — one with the estimator at top, one with reviews at top, one with a hero image.
4. Low-fi wireframe of the chosen variant with annotations; quick review with the owner focused on structure only.
5. Mid-fi wireframe with real copy, then tested with five users (next module).

### Wireframe review questions

```
[ ] Does the order match what users need to decide?
[ ] Is there one clear primary action per section?
[ ] Are objections answered before the ask?
[ ] Is anything here only because "competitors have it"?
[ ] Does it work at mobile width first?
```

### Common mistakes

- Jumping straight to high-fidelity visuals.
- Using placeholder text that hides content problems.
- Designing desktop first and cramming onto mobile.
- Un-annotated wireframes that leave behaviour to guesswork.

### Summary

Wireframe structure before style, start from a content priority list and real copy, design mobile first, annotate behaviour, and review wireframes against what users need to decide.
keyTakeaways: Wireframes agree structure and priority before visual design.
Start low-fidelity to keep feedback focused on structure.
Use real content and a content priority list rather than lorem ipsum.
Wireframe mobile first and annotate behaviour for others.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why start with low-fidelity wireframes?
options: They keep feedback focused on structure and priorities instead of colours and images
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Low fidelity avoids premature visual debates and speeds exploration.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main problem with using lorem ipsum in wireframes?
options: It hides real content problems such as long headlines or missing information
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Real content reveals layout and messaging issues early.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why wireframe the mobile version first?
options: The narrow screen forces prioritisation of what matters most
Mobile screens are easier to draw
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A narrow single-column screen forces you to decide what matters most and in what order; it is not about drawing ease, and desktop users still matter.

lessons.activity: Write a content priority list for one landing page, then sketch three different mobile layouts in 15 minutes. Turn the best into an annotated low-fidelity wireframe.

lessons.title: UI fundamentals, components and states
lessons.body:
### From wireframe to interface

Once structure is agreed, UI design makes the interface clear, consistent and attractive. For marketers, the most valuable UI knowledge is about **patterns** users already understand, **components** that can be reused, and **states** that give feedback.

### Visual hierarchy on screens

The same hierarchy principles from graphic design apply, with extra considerations:

- **One primary action per view.** Make the main button visually dominant; secondary actions look secondary (outlined or text buttons).
- **Scannable content:** headings, short paragraphs, bullet lists, bold key phrases.
- **Consistent spacing** using a scale (for example multiples of 4 or 8 px).
- **Readable text:** body text on the web commonly starts around 16 px, with comfortable line height and line length.
- **Affordances:** elements that look interactive should be interactive (buttons look tappable; links look like links).

### Common UI patterns

Users learn patterns across the web. Using familiar patterns reduces effort:

| Pattern | Use | Tips |
|---|---|---|
| Hero section | Top of landing pages | Clear headline, supporting line, CTA, relevant image |
| Cards | Products, articles, case studies | Consistent layout; whole card clickable if appropriate |
| Tabs | Switch between related views | Keep labels short; don't hide critical info |
| Accordions | FAQs, long details | Good on mobile; clear expand/collapse icons |
| Modals | Focused tasks (booking, confirm) | Easy to close; don't interrupt with them on arrival |
| Sticky CTA bar | Mobile landing pages | Don't cover content or cookie notices |
| Progress indicators | Multi-step forms, checkout | Show steps and current position |
| Toasts/snackbars | Brief confirmations | Don't use for critical errors |

### Components and design systems

A **component** is a reusable UI element: button, input, card, navigation bar. A **design system** is a collection of components, styles (colour, type, spacing), patterns and guidelines used consistently across products.

Benefits for marketing teams:

- Landing pages can be assembled quickly from approved sections.
- Consistency builds trust and brand recognition.
- Developers build faster when design matches existing components.

Many website builders and landing page tools use a section/block approach — essentially a design system. Define your own set of approved blocks: hero, social proof, features, pricing, FAQ, CTA.

### States: the forgotten half of UI

Every interactive element has states. Designing only the default state leads to confusing experiences.

```
Button states:   default | hover (desktop) | focus (keyboard) | pressed | disabled | loading
Input states:    empty | focused | filled | error | success | disabled
Page states:     loading | empty | error | success | partial data
```

Examples:

- A **loading** state on a "Pay now" button prevents double payments.
- A visible **focus** state is essential for keyboard users (and an accessibility requirement).
- **Disabled** buttons should explain why ("Fill in all required fields to continue") — or, better, keep the button enabled and show errors on submit, which is often clearer.

### Touch targets and spacing

On mobile, fingers are less precise than cursors. WCAG 2.2 includes a minimum target size criterion (generally 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exceptions), and many platform guidelines recommend larger targets (around 44–48 px) for comfort. Provide spacing between adjacent links and buttons.

### Worked example: a pricing section

Before: three plans with identical styling, eight bullet points each, "Buy" buttons in grey, and a toggle for monthly/annual that doesn't show the price change clearly.

After:

- Cards with consistent structure; the recommended plan highlighted with a label ("Most popular" — only if true).
- Short feature lists focusing on differences; full comparison in an expandable table.
- Primary button for each plan labelled "Start with Growth", etc.
- Monthly/annual toggle updates prices instantly, showing the annual saving clearly and total billed amount.
- Focus and loading states designed.

### Common mistakes

- Several equally prominent buttons competing.
- Designing only default states.
- Tiny tap targets packed together.
- Inventing unusual patterns where familiar ones work better.

### Summary

Apply hierarchy with one primary action per view, use familiar patterns, build with reusable components or approved blocks, design every state, and give touch targets enough size and spacing.
keyTakeaways: Keep one primary action per view and make secondary actions visually secondary.
Familiar UI patterns reduce effort — don't reinvent them without reason.
Reusable components or approved blocks speed up consistent landing pages.
Design all states: loading, focus, error, empty, success and disabled.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why design a loading state for a 'Pay now' button?
options: To show progress and prevent repeated taps that could cause duplicate payments
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Feedback during processing prevents confusion and double submissions.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is the best way to show secondary actions next to a primary CTA?
options: Make them equally bold and colourful
Use a less prominent style, such as an outlined or text button
Make them larger than the primary
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Visual hierarchy guides users to the main action while keeping alternatives available.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does WCAG 2.2 introduce regarding touch/click targets?
options: A minimum target size criterion, generally 24 by 24 CSS pixels with exceptions
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Target Size (Minimum) sets a baseline; many guidelines recommend larger targets for comfort.

lessons.activity: Pick one section of your site (pricing, sign-up or product card). List every state its components need and sketch the loading, error and focus states you are missing.

lessons.title: Prototyping and handoff
lessons.body:
### Testing before building

A **prototype** is an interactive simulation of an experience — clickable screens that let people try a flow before it's built. Prototypes are cheap to change; live websites and apps are not.

### Prototype fidelity

| Type | Description | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Paper prototype | Sketches you "operate" by swapping papers | Very early concept tests |
| Clickable wireframes | Low/mid-fi screens linked together | Test flows and structure |
| High-fidelity prototype | Near-final visuals, interactions, transitions | Test details, get approval, guide developers |
| Coded prototype / staging page | Real page not yet public | Test performance, real data |

Match fidelity to the question. "Can users find pricing?" needs clickable wireframes. "Does the new visual style feel premium?" needs high fidelity.

### Building a clickable prototype (tool-neutral)

In Figma-style tools, prototypes are made by linking frames with interactions:

1. Create a frame per screen or state (landing page, form, error, confirmation).
2. Add hotspots/links: "On tap → navigate to Confirmation".
3. Add overlays for modals and menus.
4. Set the device frame (e.g. a common phone size) for mobile tests.
5. Define a starting point for each flow you'll test.
6. Share a link for testing and review.

Many landing-page builders and no-code tools let you build real pages quickly too — sometimes a live unpublished page is the fastest prototype.

### What to prototype

Prototype the parts where uncertainty or risk is highest:

- New flows (booking, checkout, onboarding).
- Pages with high traffic or high spend.
- Complex interactions (filters, calculators, pricing toggles).
- Content order and messaging for key pages.

### Design handoff to developers

Handoff is where good designs get lost. Reduce friction:

```
Handoff checklist
[ ] Final designs for mobile, tablet, desktop (or defined breakpoints)
[ ] All states: hover, focus, error, loading, empty, success
[ ] Spacing, typography and colours as tokens/styles
[ ] Components named consistently with the codebase (where it exists)
[ ] Assets exported (SVG icons, optimised images) with naming
[ ] Interaction notes: animations, sticky elements, modals, scroll behaviour
[ ] Content: final copy, alt text, error messages, microcopy
[ ] Accessibility notes: heading levels, labels, focus order, contrast verified
[ ] Tracking plan: events to measure (e.g. CTA clicks, form submits)
[ ] Acceptance criteria: what "done" looks like
```

Design tools increasingly provide developer modes with measurements and code snippets, but conversations still matter. Walk developers through the flow and invite questions early.

### Working with no-code builders

Marketers often build pages themselves in website or landing-page builders. The same discipline applies:

- Build from approved sections/blocks.
- Check every breakpoint — builders often produce odd mobile layouts unless adjusted.
- Test forms end to end (does the submission arrive? is the confirmation right? does the CRM receive it?).
- Check page speed and accessibility before launch.

### Quality assurance before launch

```
Pre-launch QA
[ ] Works on at least one iOS and one Android phone, and major browsers
[ ] All links and buttons go to the right place
[ ] Forms submit, validate, confirm and store data correctly
[ ] Tracking events fire (and consent rules respected)
[ ] Page loads acceptably on mobile data
[ ] Keyboard navigation and focus visible
[ ] Spelling, prices, dates, legal text checked
[ ] Right-to-left layouts correct (if applicable)
```

### Worked example: a new checkout step

A small online shop wants to add a "gift message" option.

- Clickable prototype with two versions: checkbox that reveals a text field vs. a separate step.
- Five quick tests: the checkbox version was faster and less confusing.
- Handoff: states designed (empty, typing, character limit reached, error), copy for helper text, tracking event "gift_message_added".
- QA: tested on two phones, confirmed the message appears on the packing slip.

### Common mistakes

- Skipping prototypes for high-risk flows.
- Prototypes that only show the happy path.
- Handing over designs without states, copy or accessibility notes.
- Launching without end-to-end form and tracking tests.

### Summary

Prototype at the fidelity your question needs, focus on high-risk parts, hand off with states, tokens, copy, accessibility and tracking notes, and QA end to end before launch.
keyTakeaways: Prototypes let you test flows cheaply before building.
Match prototype fidelity to the question you're trying to answer.
Complete handoff includes states, tokens, copy, accessibility and tracking notes.
QA forms, tracking, devices and accessibility end to end before launch.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which prototype fidelity best answers 'Can users find the pricing page?'
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Findability depends on structure and labels, which clickable wireframes test quickly.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which item is most often missing from design handoffs and causes inconsistent builds?
options: Designs for all states such as error, loading and focus
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Without states, developers guess, leading to inconsistent or inaccessible behaviour.

knowledgeCheck.question: A marketer builds a landing page in a no-code builder. What must be tested before launch?
options: Mobile layouts, form submission end to end, tracking and speed
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Builders don't guarantee correct mobile layouts, data flow or performance.

lessons.activity: Build a clickable prototype of one flow (for example sign-up to confirmation) including one error state. Then write a handoff checklist for it using the template.

modules.title: Landing-page UX and mobile-first design
modules.summary: Design landing pages that match the promise, persuade ethically, load fast and work beautifully on mobile.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an effective landing page
lessons.body:
### One page, one job

A landing page is where visitors arrive from an ad, email, post or search result. The most effective landing pages have **one primary goal** — register, book, buy, download — and every element supports that goal.

### Message match

**Message match** means the landing page continues the conversation started by the ad or link. If an ad says "Free 7-day meal plan for busy parents", the page headline should echo that promise, the visuals should feel related, and the offer should be exactly the same. Poor message match makes visitors wonder if they're in the right place.

```
Message match checklist
[ ] Headline echoes the ad's promise
[ ] Same offer, price and conditions as the ad
[ ] Visual continuity (imagery, colours, style)
[ ] Same audience language (e.g. Arabic ad → Arabic page)
[ ] No bait-and-switch
```

### The core sections

| Section | Purpose | Tips |
|---|---|---|
| Hero | Instant clarity | Headline (benefit), subheadline (who/how), primary CTA, relevant visual |
| Social proof | Trust | Real testimonials, reviews, client logos with permission, numbers that are true |
| Benefits/outcomes | Why it matters | Outcomes over features; 3–6 points |
| How it works | Reduce uncertainty | 3–4 simple steps |
| Details | Answer "what exactly do I get?" | Curriculum, features, specs, inclusions |
| Pricing/offer | Decision information | Clear totals, currency, payment options, guarantees (only real ones) |
| Objections/FAQ | Remove blockers | Use real questions from customers |
| Final CTA | Easy next step | Repeat the CTA, restate the core benefit |

Not every page needs every section; short offers (a free checklist) need short pages, while high-commitment offers (a course or consultation) need more information.

### Headlines that work

A strong headline is specific and centred on the visitor's outcome:

- Weak: "Welcome to BrightPath Academy"
- Better: "Learn to edit short videos for clients in 4 weeks"
- Stronger with audience: "Freelancers: learn to edit short-form videos clients pay for — in 4 weeks"

Test headline clarity with the **five-second test**: show the page for five seconds, then ask what it offers and who it's for.

### Calls to action

- Use one primary CTA, repeated at logical points (after the hero, after proof, at the end).
- Make the CTA label specific ("Book my free call").
- Reduce risk near the CTA: "Free", "Cancel anytime", "No card needed" — only if true.
- On mobile, consider a sticky CTA bar that doesn't cover content.

### Trust and credibility

- Real testimonials with names/photos (with consent) are more credible than anonymous quotes.
- Claims must be accurate and evidenced; avoid invented numbers or "as seen in" logos without real coverage.
- Show contact details, business information, privacy policy and refund terms where relevant — these matter for trust and often for legal compliance (for example, consumer-protection and e-commerce rules requiring business identity and terms for online sales in many markets).
- Security indicators on payment pages should be genuine (reputable payment providers).

### Worked example: a free consultation page for a marketing agency in Riyadh

- Ad: "Get a free 30-minute ad account audit" (Arabic and English versions).
- Page hero (matching language): "Free 30-minute ad account audit — find wasted spend before your next campaign." CTA: "Book my free audit."
- Proof: three client testimonials with permission; certifications displayed only where genuinely held.
- What you get: a recorded audit, three priority fixes, no obligation.
- How it works: book → share read-only access → receive audit call.
- FAQ: "Do you need admin access?" "Is my data safe?" "What happens after?"
- Final CTA with scheduler embedded.

### Common mistakes

- Multiple competing goals (subscribe, follow, buy, read the blog).
- Generic headlines about the company.
- Fake scarcity or fake testimonials.
- Hiding price or key conditions until late in the process.

### Page length: how long should it be?

There is no single right length. The more a visitor has to commit — money, time or personal data — the more information they usually need before acting. A free checklist can succeed with a short page containing a headline, three benefits and a form. A high-priced course or consulting service often needs proof, detail and answers to objections. Use your research: if people keep asking the same questions before buying, the answers belong on the page.

### Summary

Give each landing page one job, match the message that brought visitors there, structure sections around decision needs, write specific outcome-focused headlines and CTAs, and build credibility with honest, evidenced proof.
keyTakeaways: Each landing page should have one primary goal.
Message match continues the ad's promise, offer, visuals and language.
Structure sections around what visitors need to decide.
Use honest, evidenced proof and clear terms to build trust.

knowledgeCheck.question: An ad promises '30% off your first order' but the landing page shows full prices with no mention of the discount. What is the problem?
options: The page has too few colours
The ad budget is too low
Poor message match, which confuses and loses visitors and may mislead
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Landing pages must continue the ad's promise; mismatched offers reduce trust and can breach advertising rules.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does a five-second test check?
options: Whether people can quickly understand what the page offers and who it's for
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A five-second test shows the page briefly and asks what it offers and for whom, testing first-impression clarity rather than speed, contrast or form completion.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which headline is strongest for a course landing page?
options: 'Freelancers: learn to edit short-form videos clients pay for — in 4 weeks'
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It names the audience, outcome and timeframe specifically.

lessons.activity: Pick one ad or post and its landing page. Run the message-match checklist and a five-second test with two people, then rewrite the headline and primary CTA.

lessons.title: Mobile-first design
lessons.body:
### Most of your visitors are on phones

For traffic from social media, messaging apps and many email campaigns, mobile devices are often the majority. Mobile-first design means designing for small screens, touch input and variable connections **first**, then enhancing for larger screens.

### Why mobile first works

- **Forces prioritisation:** one column means you must decide what matters most.
- **Improves performance:** fewer, lighter elements.
- **Aligns with how search engines evaluate sites:** Google uses mobile-first indexing, primarily using the mobile version of content for indexing and ranking.
- **Reflects real usage:** in many markets, including Pakistan, the Gulf and much of the world, mobile is the main or only way many people access the internet.

### Mobile design principles

| Principle | Practice |
|---|---|
| Thumb-friendly | Key actions reachable; large targets (at least WCAG's minimum, ideally around 44–48 px); spacing between links |
| Readable | Body text around 16 px or larger; short paragraphs; sufficient contrast |
| Scannable | Clear headings, bullets, accordions for detail |
| Fast | Compressed images, limited scripts, avoid heavy video backgrounds |
| Focused | One primary CTA; simplified navigation |
| Forgiving | Easy to correct mistakes; autofill; appropriate keyboards |
| Context-aware | Tap-to-call, WhatsApp links, maps, wallet payments where relevant |

### Responsive layouts and breakpoints

Responsive design adapts layouts to screen width:

- **Mobile:** single column, stacked sections, full-width buttons.
- **Tablet:** two columns where helpful.
- **Desktop:** multi-column layouts, side-by-side images and text.

Decide how each section transforms: a three-card row becomes a stack or a horizontal swipe; a comparison table becomes stacked cards or a scrollable table with a sticky first column.

### Forms on mobile

- Single column fields.
- Correct input types (email, tel, number) to show the right keyboard.
- Autocomplete attributes so browsers can fill details.
- Minimal typing: selectors, toggles, smart defaults.
- Keep the submit button visible and clearly labelled.
- Show errors inline and near the field.
- Allow wallet payments and local payment methods where relevant.

### Mobile-specific pitfalls

- **Intrusive interstitials:** full-screen pop-ups on arrival frustrate users and can hurt search visibility; Google has guidance against intrusive interstitials on mobile.
- **Sticky elements** (headers, chat bubbles, cookie banners, CTA bars) stacking up and covering content.
- **Hover-dependent** interactions that don't work on touch.
- **Tiny text in images** (infographics that are unreadable on phones).
- **Horizontal scrolling** caused by oversized elements.

### In-app browsers

Many visitors from social platforms open links in the app's built-in browser. These can behave differently: autofill may be limited, users may not be logged in to other services, and some payment or login flows break. Test your key flows from within the major social apps your audience uses.

### Testing on real devices

Emulators in browser developer tools are helpful, but test on real phones too — including a mid-range Android device on a mobile connection, which reflects many users' reality better than a flagship phone on office Wi-Fi.

```
Mobile QA checklist
[ ] Hero message and CTA visible quickly
[ ] Text readable without zoom
[ ] Tap targets comfortable; no accidental taps
[ ] No horizontal scrolling
[ ] Sticky elements don't cover content
[ ] Forms use correct keyboards and autofill
[ ] Works inside social in-app browsers
[ ] Acceptable load time on mobile data
```

### Worked example: a restaurant ordering page

Before: desktop-designed menu with small text, a PDF menu link, hover-to-see prices, and a phone number that wasn't tappable.

After: mobile-first menu with categories as sticky tabs; dishes as cards with photos, prices and "Add" buttons; tap-to-call and WhatsApp buttons; an Arabic/English language switch; checkout with wallet payments and cash-on-delivery options where relevant.

### Common mistakes

- Designing on desktop and "shrinking" to mobile.
- PDF menus or brochures as the main content.
- Stacking multiple sticky elements.
- Testing only on flagship phones and fast Wi-Fi.

### Performance budgets for mobile

Set a simple performance budget for campaign pages — for example a maximum total page weight, a limit on third-party scripts, and a target for how quickly the main content appears on a mid-range phone. Check it before every launch. Budgets make trade-offs visible: adding a chat widget or tracking pixel then becomes a deliberate decision rather than something that quietly slows the page.

### Summary

Design for small screens, touch and variable connections first; prioritise one column; make forms and targets thumb-friendly; avoid intrusive pop-ups and sticky clutter; test in in-app browsers and on real mid-range devices.
keyTakeaways: Mobile-first design forces prioritisation and reflects how most social traffic arrives.
Make targets thumb-friendly, text readable and forms easy with correct keyboards and autofill.
Avoid intrusive interstitials and stacked sticky elements.
Test on real mid-range phones, mobile data and social in-app browsers.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why test landing pages inside social apps' in-app browsers?
options: They can behave differently, breaking autofill, logins or payments
knowledgeCheck.explanation: In-app browsers have quirks that can break key flows.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is a mobile-first practice for forms?
options: Correct input types and autocomplete so the right keyboard and autofill appear
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Input types and autocomplete reduce typing effort and errors.

knowledgeCheck.question: A page shows a full-screen pop-up immediately on mobile. What is the likely effect?
options: Frustration and potential negative impact on search visibility
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Intrusive interstitials frustrate users and are discouraged by search guidance.

lessons.activity: Open your key landing page on a mid-range phone using mobile data, and from inside one social app. Run the mobile QA checklist and fix the top three issues.

lessons.title: Speed, trust and ethical persuasion
lessons.body:
### Three silent conversion killers

Visitors rarely complain about slow pages, hidden fees or manipulative tricks — they just leave, or they buy once and never return. This lesson covers performance, trust and the difference between ethical persuasion and dark patterns.

### Performance

Slow pages lose visitors, especially on mobile connections. Google's **Core Web Vitals** measure key aspects of user experience:

| Metric | Measures | Common causes of poor scores |
|---|---|---|
| Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) | How quickly the main content appears | Huge images, slow servers, render-blocking scripts |
| Interaction to Next Paint (INP) | How quickly the page responds to interactions | Heavy JavaScript, too many third-party scripts |
| Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) | Visual stability | Images without dimensions, late-loading banners, ads |

Practical fixes for marketers:

- Compress and correctly size images; use modern formats (e.g. WebP/AVIF) where supported.
- Avoid autoplay background videos on mobile, or use very light versions.
- Limit tracking pixels, chat widgets and third-party scripts — each adds weight.
- Reserve space for images and embeds to prevent layout shifts.
- Use tools like PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse to diagnose, and test on real devices.

### Trust signals

Trust determines whether visitors are willing to act.

```
Trust checklist
[ ] Clear business identity (name, location/contact, registration details where relevant)
[ ] Real testimonials and reviews (with consent), not cherry-picked to mislead
[ ] Transparent pricing including taxes, fees and delivery costs
[ ] Clear refund/cancellation terms
[ ] Privacy policy and cookie information
[ ] Secure, reputable payment options (including locally trusted methods)
[ ] Consistent, professional design and error-free copy
[ ] Responsive support channel (chat, email, WhatsApp)
```

### Persuasion versus manipulation

Persuasion helps people make decisions that are good for them by making benefits, proof and next steps clear. **Dark patterns** (also called deceptive design) trick or pressure people into actions they wouldn't otherwise take.

| Dark pattern | Example | Ethical alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Fake urgency | Countdown timer that resets on refresh | Real deadlines, stated honestly |
| Fake scarcity | "Only 2 left!" when untrue | Accurate stock levels |
| Confirmshaming | "No thanks, I don't like saving money" | Neutral decline option: "No thanks" |
| Sneak into basket | Pre-added insurance or add-ons | Opt-in add-ons |
| Hidden costs | Fees appear only at the last step | All-in price shown early |
| Roach motel | Easy sign-up, very hard cancellation | Cancellation as easy as sign-up |
| Forced continuity | Free trial silently converts with no reminder | Reminder before charging, easy cancel |
| Pre-ticked consent | Marketing consent pre-selected | Unticked, specific consent |
| Disguised ads | Ads that look like content or reviews | Clear labelling |

Regulators increasingly target these practices. For example, the US FTC has acted against deceptive design and subscription traps; the UK's consumer-protection framework has been strengthened with new enforcement powers and rules on fake reviews and drip pricing; and the EU's Digital Services Act and consumer laws address manipulative interfaces. Similar consumer-protection principles apply in the Gulf and South Asia. Beyond legal risk, dark patterns damage trust, increase refunds and chargebacks, and hurt long-term customer value.

### Cookie consent UX

Where consent is required (for example under GDPR and the UK's rules for non-essential cookies), consent banners must offer genuine choice. Good practice: "Accept" and "Reject" options with equal prominence, clear categories, no pre-ticked boxes, and an easy way to change preferences later. Design banners so they don't block key content excessively on mobile.

### Ethical persuasion toolkit

- **Clarity:** specific benefits and honest outcomes.
- **Social proof:** real reviews, representative results.
- **Authority:** genuine credentials, real media coverage.
- **Reciprocity:** useful free content before asking.
- **Risk reversal:** real guarantees, easy cancellation.
- **Commitment:** small first steps (a free call, a trial) with transparent terms.

### Worked example: subscription sign-up

Before: price shown as "from $9" with a $29 setup fee revealed at checkout; annual plan pre-selected; cancellation by email only; timer "Offer ends in 10:00" resetting.

After: full price and setup fee shown upfront; monthly/annual choice with clear totals; cancellation in account settings; reminder email before renewal; honest launch discount with a real end date. Complaints and refund requests are then monitored alongside conversion rate.

### Common mistakes

- Adding scripts and widgets without checking performance.
- Hiding fees to make prices look lower.
- Using manipulative copy and fake timers.
- Cookie banners designed to push "Accept all".

### Summary

Optimise performance using Core Web Vitals as a guide, build trust with transparency, and persuade ethically — avoiding dark patterns that increasingly attract regulatory action and erode long-term customer value.
keyTakeaways: Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) measure loading, responsiveness and visual stability.
Limit heavy media and third-party scripts; reserve space to avoid layout shifts.
Trust comes from transparency: identity, real proof, full pricing and clear terms.
Avoid dark patterns — they harm trust and increasingly attract regulatory enforcement.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which Core Web Vital measures visual stability?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: CLS measures unexpected layout movement; LCP measures loading of main content; INP measures responsiveness.

knowledgeCheck.question: A countdown timer resets every time the page is refreshed. What is this?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Timers that aren't real deadlines create false urgency and can mislead consumers.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is good practice for cookie consent banners where consent is required?
options: Hiding the reject option in settings
Accept and reject options with equal prominence and no pre-ticked categories
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Genuine choice requires comparable prominence and no pre-selection.

lessons.activity: Run PageSpeed Insights (or a similar tool) on one landing page and fix one issue. Then audit the page and checkout for the dark patterns in the table and replace any you find with ethical alternatives.

modules.title: Accessibility essentials (WCAG basics)
modules.summary: Understand WCAG 2.2 principles and levels, apply a practical accessibility checklist to marketing content, and test with tools and assistive technology.

lessons.title: WCAG principles, levels and why they matter
lessons.body:
### Accessibility is for everyone

Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with your content. This includes people who are blind or have low vision, are deaf or hard of hearing, have motor impairments, cognitive or learning disabilities, or temporary and situational limitations (a broken arm, bright sunlight, a noisy environment). The World Health Organization estimates that around 1.3 billion people — about one in six people worldwide — experience significant disability. Accessible design also improves usability for everyone.

### The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines

The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)**, published by the W3C, are the internationally recognised standard. **WCAG 2.2** (published in 2023) is the current version; it builds on 2.0 and 2.1, so meeting 2.2 generally satisfies earlier versions too. WCAG 3 is in development but not yet a standard.

### The four principles: POUR

| Principle | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Perceivable | Information can be perceived by at least one sense | Alt text, captions, sufficient contrast, text that can be resized |
| Operable | Interface can be operated by various means | Keyboard access, enough time, no seizure-inducing flashes, target sizes |
| Understandable | Content and operation are understandable | Clear language, predictable behaviour, helpful error messages |
| Robust | Works with current and future technologies, including assistive tech | Valid, semantic code; proper names and roles for controls |

### Conformance levels

- **Level A:** the minimum; failures create severe barriers.
- **Level AA:** the level most laws, policies and organisations target. It includes contrast (4.5:1 for normal text), captions for prerecorded video, visible focus, and more.
- **Level AAA:** enhanced; not usually required for entire sites because some criteria can't be met for all content.

**Target WCAG 2.2 AA** as your standard.

### What WCAG 2.2 added

Useful to know, as they affect marketing pages and forms:

- **Focus Not Obscured (Minimum, AA):** keyboard focus shouldn't be completely hidden by sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets.
- **Dragging Movements (AA):** functionality that uses dragging (like sliders) needs a simple alternative (such as tapping).
- **Target Size (Minimum, AA):** interactive targets generally at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels, or with enough spacing, with some exceptions.
- **Consistent Help (A):** help mechanisms (contact links, chat) appear in a consistent place across pages.
- **Redundant Entry (A):** don't make users re-enter information they already provided in the same process.
- **Accessible Authentication (Minimum, AA):** don't require cognitive tests like remembering or transcribing passwords without alternatives (allow paste and password managers, for example).

### Legal and business context

Accessibility is increasingly a legal requirement, though specifics vary:

- **European Union:** the European Accessibility Act applies from June 2025 to many products and services, including e-commerce, with standards aligned to WCAG.
- **United Kingdom:** the Equality Act requires reasonable adjustments; public-sector bodies have specific website accessibility regulations.
- **United States:** the ADA has been applied to websites in many legal cases, and federal rules set WCAG-based requirements for state and local government websites.
- **Other markets:** many countries, including in the Gulf, have disability rights laws and government digital accessibility policies; requirements for private businesses vary.

Check requirements for the markets you serve and your sector. Regardless of law, accessible sites reach more customers and are usually better for SEO and usability.
